section.title: One in Christ
section.sectionRationale: Having shown that every believer, whether Jew or Gentile, is saved by grace through faith and not by works, Paul now turns to the great social and cosmic result of that grace. The vertical reconciliation of sinners to God in chapter two produces a horizontal reconciliation of former enemies to one another. The deepest division in the ancient world, the wall between Jew and Gentile, is torn down at the cross, and out of the two God creates one new humanity that is being built into a temple where He Himself dwells.
section.thesis: Those who were once far off, without Christ, without hope, and without God, have been brought near by the blood of Christ, who is Himself our peace: by His death He abolished the dividing wall, made the two into one new man, reconciled both to God in one body, and now builds Jew and Gentile together into a holy temple, a dwelling place for God in the Spirit.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the Gentiles remembered in their former estate, once far off and without hope; the peace made by the blood of Christ, who tears down the wall and creates one new man with access to the Father; and the new household of God, built on the apostolic foundation with Christ as cornerstone into a holy temple.

verses.text: Therefore remember that formerly you who are Gentiles in the flesh and called uncircumcised by the so-called circumcision (that done in the body by human hands),
remember that at that time you were separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of the promise, without hope and without God in the world.

units.label: Brought near, our peace, one new man
units.note: reconciled by the blood of Christ

verses.text: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ.
For He Himself is our {{eirene|peace}}, who has made the two one and has torn down the {{mesotoichon|dividing wall}} of hostility
by abolishing in His flesh the law of commandments and decrees. He did this to create in Himself one new man out of the two, thus making peace
and {{apokatallasso|reconciling}} both of them to God in one body through the cross, by which He put to death their hostility.
He came and preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near.
For through Him we both have {{prosagoge|access}} to the Father by one Spirit.
Therefore you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household,
built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the {{akrogoniaios|cornerstone}}.
In Him the whole building is fitted together and grows into a holy {{naos|temple}} in the Lord.
And in Him you too are being built together into a {{katoiketerion|dwelling place}} for God in His Spirit.

eirene.gloss: Peace, wholeness, the restored well-being that comes when hostility is ended and relationship is made right. It carries the fullness of the Hebrew shalom. Paul does not merely say Christ makes peace or gives peace; He Himself is our peace, His own person the meeting point where God and man, Jew and Gentile, are joined. The peace is not a treaty negotiated between two parties but a new reality created in Him.

mesotoichon.gloss: A middle wall, a dividing partition. The image likely recalls the barrier in the Jerusalem temple that separated the court of the Gentiles from the inner courts, past which no Gentile could go on pain of death. It also pictures the whole system of law and custom that fenced Israel off from the nations. Paul says Christ has torn it down, so that the very structure that kept the outsider outside is demolished at the cross.

apokatallasso.gloss: To reconcile fully, to restore a broken relationship to peace. Here the reconciliation is twofold: Jew and Gentile are reconciled to each other and both together are reconciled to God in one body through the cross. The same word crowns the Christ hymn in Colossians 1:20, where God reconciles all things by the blood of the cross. Reconciliation is God's work, achieved at cost, not a peace the estranged parties broker for themselves.

prosagoge.gloss: Access, the right and freedom to approach, the act of being led into the presence of a king. Through Christ both Jew and Gentile have this access to the Father by one Spirit. The word gathers up the whole Trinity into one clause: we come to the Father, through the Son, in the one Spirit. What the temple wall once forbade the Gentile is now opened wide to all who are in Christ.

akrogoniaios.gloss: The cornerstone, or the chief capstone, the decisive foundation stone that sets the line and bears the weight of the whole building, binding its walls together. Christ Jesus Himself is this stone, fulfilling Isaiah 28:16 and Psalm 118:22. The apostles and prophets form the foundation, but Christ is the stone on which everything is aligned and held; remove Him and the structure has no coherence.

naos.gloss: The temple, and specifically the inner sanctuary, the holy dwelling where God's presence rests, not merely the outer temple precincts. Paul says the church, Jew and Gentile joined in Christ, is growing into this holy naos in the Lord. The place of God's dwelling is no longer a building of stone in one city but a people knit together in Christ across every nation.

katoiketerion.gloss: A dwelling place, a settled habitation, a permanent home. The word speaks not of a passing visit but of God taking up lasting residence. The reconciled people are being built together into a katoiketerion for God in His Spirit, the fulfilment of the ancient promise that God would dwell in the midst of His people, now realised by the indwelling Spirit in the church.

basic.context: Paul tells the Gentile believers to remember what they once were: outsiders to Israel, strangers to God's promises, without hope and without God in the world. Then comes the great turn, but now. In Christ Jesus those who were far away have been brought near by His blood. Jesus Himself is their peace. At the cross He tore down the wall that divided Jew and Gentile, made the two into one new humanity, and reconciled both to God in one body. Now they are no longer foreigners but fellow citizens and family, built together into a temple where God Himself lives by His Spirit.
basic.hermeneutics: The passage moves in three beats: the bleak former state of the Gentiles, verses 11 to 12; the peace won at the cross, verses 13 to 18; and the new temple built out of former enemies, verses 19 to 22. The hinge is the phrase but now in verse 13. Paul argues from what God has done in Christ to what the church now is, so the unity of the church is not a goal to achieve by effort but a fact created by the cross to be lived out.
basic.originalLanguages: Christ Himself is our eirene, our peace, the Hebrew shalom embodied in a person. He tore down the mesotoichon, the dividing wall, likely echoing the temple barrier that kept Gentiles out. He is apokatallasso, the one who reconciles both to God in one body. Through Him we have prosagoge, access to the Father by one Spirit. He is the akrogoniaios, the cornerstone that aligns the whole building, which grows into a holy naos, a sanctuary, a katoiketerion, a dwelling place for God in the Spirit.
basic.typology: The temple, its dividing wall, and its holy sanctuary all find their meaning here. The barrier that once shut the Gentile out is torn down in Christ, and the sanctuary where God dwelt is fulfilled in the church, a living temple of Jew and Gentile joined together. The covenants and promises made to Israel are opened to the nations in the one to whom they always pointed.
basic.christ: Christ is not merely the peacemaker; He Himself is our peace. He is the one who brings the far-off near by His blood, who abolishes the dividing wall in His flesh, who creates one new man in Himself, who reconciles both to God through the cross, and who is the cornerstone on whom the whole temple rises. Every clause centres on His person and His death.
basic.god: God is the one who was once far from the nations and now, through the cross, draws near to them. He is the God who reconciles enemies, both to Himself and to one another, and who chooses to dwell not in a building of stone but in a people. The passage shows a God whose purpose was always to gather one people for His own presence.
basic.crossReferences: Colossians 1 speaks of the same reconciliation of all things by the blood of the cross. Isaiah 57 promises peace to the far and the near. Galatians 3 declares that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek. 1 Peter 2 calls believers living stones built into a spiritual house.
basic.oneStory: From Abraham, God promised to bless all nations through his seed. Israel was set apart, fenced off by law and temple, to guard the promise until the seed came. Now in Christ the wall comes down and the nations are brought in, one new humanity built into the temple God always meant to fill with His presence. The story runs from a garden where God walked with man to a people in whom God now dwells by His Spirit.

context.literary:
Verses 11 to 22 are one long Greek sentence in the first half and a second in the second, and both are built on contrasts. The passage is held together by a pair of imperatives and a pair of pronouns. 'Remember' opens it in verse 11 and is repeated in verse 12, and the whole of verses 11 and 12 is a catalogue of negatives: separate, alienated, strangers, without hope, without God. Then the weight swings on the little phrase 'But now' in verse 13. Verses 14 to 18 are packed with first and third person, 'He Himself', 'in His flesh', 'in Himself', 'through Him', while the readers move between 'you' and 'we'. In verse 17 Paul says 'you who were far away', and in verse 18 he says 'we both', and by verse 19 'you' has become 'fellow citizens'. The pronoun changes are the argument in small.

Notice how often the sentence says 'two' and 'one'. The two become one in verse 14, one new man out of the two in verse 15, both reconciled in one body in verse 16, we both have access by one Spirit in verse 18. Paul does not blend the two peoples into a third thing that erases them; he says both are reconciled and both have access. Verses 19 to 22 then change the picture from a divided courtyard to a building. Citizens, household, foundation, cornerstone, structure, temple: the metaphors stack from city to family to architecture, and the last two verbs, 'fitted together' and 'being built together', are in the present tense, so the building is still going up.

The passage also looks back and forward. 'Peace' is the thread, appearing in verses 14, 15, 17 twice. It echoes the prayer of 1:2 and prepares for the call to keep 'the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace' in 4:3.
context.historical:
Paul is writing to a church that was mostly Gentile in a city dominated by the temple of Artemis. Most of its members had grown up with no share in Israel's Scriptures. Verse 11 reminds them that Jews called them 'the uncircumcision', a label that sounded like an insult, and Paul quietly qualifies the other side too: the 'so-called circumcision' is only that done in the body by human hands. He does not deny that circumcision was God's sign; he says that the mark in the flesh without the heart was never the point, a theme he takes up in Romans 2:28 to 29.

The wall of verse 14 is almost certainly more than a metaphor. Josephus describes a low stone barrier in the Jerusalem temple that kept Gentiles out of the inner courts, with notices in Greek and Latin warning of death for a foreigner who crossed it. Paul had felt the force of that barrier himself. In Acts 21:28 to 29 a mob in Jerusalem seized him because they supposed he had brought Trophimus, an Ephesian, past it. The Ephesians who first heard this letter may have known that story. Paul is writing as a prisoner in Rome, and he tells them that the wall which nearly killed him has already been torn down by Christ.

The wider world matters too. Rome prided itself on holding diverse peoples under one peace, the Pax Romana, and its emperors were hailed as peace bringers. Paul says the true peace was made by a crucified Jew, and that it created a people no empire could assemble: former enemies sharing a table and a household. The phrase 'fellow citizens' would have carried weight in a Roman world where citizenship was precious and unequal.
context.canonical:
The Old Testament already had a place for the nations, which is why Paul's claim is a fulfilment and not an innovation. The promise to Abraham was that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, Genesis 12:3. Solomon prayed at the dedication of the temple that the foreigner who prayed toward it would be heard, so that all the peoples would know God's name, 1 Kings 8:41 to 43. Isaiah promised that the foreigners who joined themselves to the LORD would be brought to His holy mountain, and that His house would be called a house of prayer for all the nations, Isaiah 56:6 to 7. The prophets also spoke of a future peace for those far and near, Isaiah 57:19, which Paul quotes in spirit at verse 17.

Within the New Testament the passage belongs with Romans 15:7 to 12, where Paul gathers a chain of Old Testament texts to show that the Gentiles were always meant to praise God with His people, and with Galatians 3:28, which says that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek. It runs close to Colossians 1:20 to 22, which also speaks of peace through the blood of the cross and of former alienation overcome.

The temple language reaches back to the tabernacle and forward to Revelation. Paul says the church is the place where God now dwells, a thought shared with 1 Corinthians 3:16 to 17 and 1 Peter 2:4 to 6. The Bible ends with the voice from the throne announcing that God's dwelling place is with man, Revelation 21:3, and there is no temple building in that city, Revelation 21:22.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants Gentile believers to do two things at once. First, he wants them to remember accurately, without exaggerating their past and without forgetting it, because gratitude depends on memory. The word 'remember' is a present imperative: keep on remembering. Second, he wants them to see that the unity of the church is not a diplomatic arrangement between two parties who agreed to tolerate each other. It was created by one death, in one body, by one Spirit, and so it cannot be renegotiated.

There is also a pastoral edge for the Jewish believers who may have been reading over their shoulders. Paul never says the Gentiles have become Jews. He says that both have come to God through Christ, and that the one new man is formed 'out of the two'. Neither group is the guest of the other. Both are guests of the Father, and both are members of His household.

Finally, Paul is preparing a base for the practical chapters. In chapter 4 he will ask the same people to keep the unity of the Spirit. He can only ask that because he has first said what God has already done. The command grows out of the declaration.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The verbs of verses 13 to 18 are all in the past: brought near, made, torn down, abolished, extinguished. These describe what Christ did and are not instructions to be carried out. The only direct command in the passage is 'remember' in verse 11, and what follows is the content of what to remember. The verbs of verses 21 and 22 are present and ongoing, growing and being built, which describes a process God is carrying out.

It would therefore be a mistake to read this passage as a programme for the church to build unity. The church does not build the wall's removal; it lives in a world where the wall is already gone. What the passage does require is that the church stop rebuilding it. When congregations divide by ethnicity, class or background and treat that as normal, they are putting up what Christ tore down. The application is to let the finished work show up in how we welcome, worship and eat together, as Paul argues in Galatians 2:11 to 14.

debates.question: What did Christ abolish when He abolished 'the law of commandments and decrees'?

views.label: The ceremonial and boundary-marking commands of Israel
views.case: Paul's wall is the hostility that separated two peoples, and the commands that did the separating were circumcision, food laws and festival observance, Leviticus 20:24 to 26. Verse 15 says Christ abolished them 'in His flesh', and Colossians 2:14 to 17 speaks similarly of the decrees against us and of food, festivals and Sabbaths as shadows. On this reading the moral law is not in view, and Paul himself says elsewhere that love fulfils it, Romans 13:8 to 10.

views.label: The law as a system of condemnation and separation
views.case: Others take 'law' as the whole Mosaic covenant in its role as a standard that condemned and fenced Israel off. At the cross its demands were met and its penalty borne, so it no longer stands as a barrier either between God and sinners or between Jew and Gentile. The word translated 'decrees' is dogmasin, which in Colossians 2:14 appears in the phrase about the debt ascribed to us in the decrees that stood against us.

debates.bearing: Both views agree on what matters for this passage: the commandments no longer serve as a border, and nobody has to cross one to belong to God's people. The disagreement only concerns how much of the Mosaic law is covered, and the verse does not try to settle every question about the law's ongoing role.

debates.question: Who is the 'one new man' of verse 15?

views.label: A corporate humanity, the church as a new people
views.case: The phrase is 'one new man out of the two', and verse 16 immediately speaks of 'one body'. In Paul's thought Adam and Christ stand for whole peoples, Romans 5:12 to 21, so the new man is a new humanity formed in Christ, which is how Ephesians 4:24 also speaks of putting on a new self.

views.label: Christ Himself, with believers included in Him
views.case: The 'in Himself' of verse 15 suggests the new humanity is made in Christ and is inseparable from Him. Some therefore stress that the one new man is Christ as head with His body, and not simply an abstraction about the church.

debates.bearing: The two readings are not far apart. Whether the emphasis falls on the people or on the person, the new humanity exists only in Christ, and it is one, not two peoples sitting side by side.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with the word for 'remember' in verse 11. Mnemoneuete is a present imperative, which suggests continued remembering and not a single recollection. Paul does not want the Ephesians to wallow in their past but to let it shape their thanks, and the same verb in Acts 20:31 shows Paul using it to ground a pastoral appeal in memory.

In verse 12 Paul says the Gentiles were alienated from the 'commonwealth' of Israel. The Greek behind commonwealth is politeia, the word for a citizen body with its own laws and rights. It is a political term, and Paul uses it so that verse 19 can answer it with sympolitai, 'fellow citizens'. The prefix syn, 'with', recurs across this passage and in Ephesians 3:6, where Paul says the Gentiles are fellow heirs and fellow members. It is Paul's way of insisting that the Gentiles come in as full partners and not as appendages.

Verse 19 names two kinds of outsider: xenoi and paroikoi, 'strangers and foreigners'. A xenos is a stranger passing through; a paroikos is a resident alien, living in a place without a citizen's rights. Both are then replaced by an insider term, oikeioi, 'members of God's household', built on oikos, the household. The shift is from a legal status to a family one, so that the Gentiles are not just admitted to the city but welcomed in at home.

In verse 15 Paul says 'one new man', and the word for new is kainos. Greek has another word, neos, meaning new in time, recent. Kainos means new in kind or quality, something that did not exist before. So the new man is not a repaired old Jew or an improved old Gentile, but a humanity of a different kind. The verb for 'create' is ktizo, used for the original creation, which suggests the cross is a work of new creation, as 2 Corinthians 5:17 also says.

Verse 18 speaks of 'access', prosagoge. The same word appears in Romans 5:2 and Ephesians 3:12. It names the right of approach to a person of rank, and in the ancient world one might speak of being introduced into a king's presence. Paul adds that this approach is 'through Him', 'to the Father', 'by one Spirit', which gives all three persons a place in a single sentence.

Finally, the builder's words in verses 20 to 22. 'Cornerstone' is akrogoniaios, the same word the Septuagint uses at Isaiah 28:16. Two verbs of building follow, 'fitted together' in verse 21 and 'being built together' in verse 22, both present tense, both carrying the prefix syn. The structure is a joint effort of many stones, and Christ is the one who keeps them aligned.

typology.type: The dividing wall of the temple, Ephesians 2:14
typology.fulfillment: The Jerusalem temple kept the nations in an outer court, and a barrier warned them not to go further, which Acts 21:28 to 29 shows was still enforced in Paul's day. At the cross Christ tore down the wall of hostility and brought Jew and Gentile into the one presence. The escalation is from a courtyard that excluded to a body that includes, and the veil that separated God from His people was torn at His death, Matthew 27:51. Hebrews 10:19 to 20 says the way into the Most Holy Place is opened through the curtain of His body. The type falls short because a wall is a place; Christ is a person, and access through Him is not limited to Jerusalem.

typology.type: The temple as dwelling place, Ephesians 2:21 to 22
typology.fulfillment: God's presence filled the tabernacle and then Solomon's temple, 1 Kings 8:10 to 11, but both were buildings that people entered from outside. Paul says God now builds a temple out of persons, and that God dwells in it by His Spirit. Jesus had already spoken of the temple of His own body, John 2:19 to 21, and Paul teaches elsewhere that the church is God's temple, 1 Corinthians 3:16 to 17. The type falls short because the old temple had to be rebuilt and could be destroyed, while this temple is still growing and cannot be torn down, Matthew 16:18.

typology.type: The stone laid in Zion, Ephesians 2:20
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 28:16 speaks of a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, laid in Zion as a sure foundation. Psalm 118:22 says the builders rejected a stone that became the cornerstone. Peter applies both to Jesus, 1 Peter 2:4 to 6. Paul adds that the apostles and prophets are the foundation, with Christ as the cornerstone that sets the line for everything else. The type falls short in that an ordinary cornerstone is lifeless and silent; Christ is the living stone who also lives in the building and gives it its life.

typology.type: The covenant of peace, Ephesians 2:14 to 17
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel 37:26 to 27 promises a covenant of peace and a sanctuary among the people, with God's dwelling with them. Isaiah 52:7 praises the feet of the one who proclaims peace, and Isaiah 57:19 says peace to those far and near. Paul says Christ Himself came and preached this peace to both groups, and that He is it. The escalation is from a promise that peace would come to a person who is the peace. The type falls short because the prophets looked for peace and restoration for Israel and the nations in the future; Paul says the beginning of it is here, though its full display awaits the new creation.

study.christ:
Every verb of verses 13 to 18 has Christ as its subject, and Paul keeps pressing the point that He does it personally: 'He Himself is our peace', 'in His flesh', 'in Himself', 'through the cross', 'He came and preached'. This is more than saying Christ brings peace. He is peace in person, so that to be near Him is to be at peace, and to be far from Him is to be at war.

The passage shows three stages in His work. First, the cross removes the cause of hostility. The wall between the peoples was real, but so was the wall between each of them and God, and verse 16 says the cross dealt with both at once. Colossians 1:20 says He made peace through the blood of His cross, and Romans 5:1 says that, justified by faith, we have peace with God. Reconciliation with God and reconciliation with one another are not two projects with a link between them; they are one event.

Second, He 'came and preached peace' in verse 17. Paul does not say He did this during His earthly ministry alone. Most commentators take it as a reference to the risen Christ proclaiming peace through the apostles and the Spirit, which fits the allusion to Isaiah 52:7 and 57:19. The risen Lord still speaks peace to Jew and Gentile, to the near and the far, and does so through the gospel.

Third, He is the cornerstone, the stone that sets the line for the whole building. This carries the Old Testament stone texts into the church. Isaiah 28:16 promised that the one who believes would never be shaken, and 1 Peter 2:6 quotes it of Jesus. What the Jerusalem builders rejected, Psalm 118:22, is the stone that now holds the house together.

We should guard against over-allegorising. Paul does not say the temple wall was a type of Christ's body in every detail, and the passage does not say the Jewish people have been replaced. The link is fulfilment of purposes: Christ's cross fulfilled what the wall was meant to protect and then removed what it kept out. Hebrews 10:19 to 20 explains how: the new and living way is opened through the curtain of His body. Jesus said He had other sheep not of this fold, and that there would be one flock and one shepherd, John 10:16. Ephesians 2 shows how that happens.
study.god:
The first thing the passage shows about God is that He is the one who makes the first move. The Gentiles were 'without God in the world', and nothing in them brought them near. Paul says they 'have been brought near', a passive verb: someone else did the bringing. The initiative is the Father's, carried out by the Son, applied by the Spirit. This is the same pattern as 1:3 to 14, now seen in a social key.

The passage also shows God as a peacemaker who does not simply ignore the offence. Peace is made 'through the blood of Christ' and 'through the cross', not by saying that hostility does not matter. Verse 16 says the cross extinguished the hostility, and the verb suggests killing it. Divine peace is not a truce; it is the end of a war by the death of the one who bore its cost. This holds together two things that can seem to pull apart, God's holiness, which does not wink at sin, and His love, which will not abandon the far off.

A third thing: God is one God of both peoples. Paul argues the same in Romans 3:29 to 30, where he asks whether God is the God of Jews only, and answers that He is the God of Gentiles too, since there is only one God. The one God makes one people. A tribal god would be content with a tribal people, but this God cannot be content with less than all the families of the earth, Genesis 12:3.

Fourth, God chooses to dwell with His people. In verse 22 Paul says the church is 'a dwelling place for God in His Spirit'. Moses had said that no other nation had a god as near as the LORD was to Israel, Deuteronomy 4:7; Paul says that nearness has now been extended. God is not far, and it is His chosen way to be present among a community of forgiven enemies rather than in a building.

The passage also affects how we worship. Paul puts the Trinity at the centre in verse 18: access to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. Prayer is therefore not an attempt to reach a distant deity but an approach already made possible. It also means worship is never merely private. Those who come near come together, and a church that welcomes only people like itself is denying what God has said about Himself.

crossReferences.note: The promise behind verse 17. The LORD says, 'Peace, peace to those far and near.' Paul says Christ came and preached peace to those far away and to those near, so he reads the prophecy as fulfilled in the gospel. Note that Isaiah puts the far first, as Paul does.

The messenger whose feet are beautiful on the mountains proclaims peace and salvation. Paul's 'He came and preached peace' in verse 17 draws on this, so the one who brings good news is also the good news. Ephesians 6:15 later calls the gospel the gospel of peace.

A mob accuses Paul of bringing Greeks into the temple, having seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him. It shows that the wall was still a living boundary when Paul wrote and that Paul had almost died for crossing it. His words in verse 14 about it being torn down are therefore costly words.

A parallel account of reconciliation. Christ makes peace through the blood of His cross, and those once alienated and hostile are now reconciled in His physical body through death. Colossians widens the scope to all things, while Ephesians draws out the social result for Jew and Gentile.

Paul's baptismal slogan, which lists three pairs of opposites and puts them all under Christ. Ephesians 2 supplies the argument behind the slogan: the cross removed the wall, so ancestry no longer decides anyone's place among God's people.

Paul gathers four Old Testament texts to show that the Gentiles were always meant to praise God with His people, and ends with the Root of Jesse in whom the Gentiles will hope. It shows that Ephesians 2 is not a late novelty but the realisation of a scriptural hope.

God lays a tested, precious cornerstone in Zion, a sure foundation, and says the one who believes will never be shaken. Paul's cornerstone in verse 20 comes from this text, which Peter also quotes in 1 Peter 2:6. The Septuagint word akrogoniaios is the one Paul uses.

Believers, like living stones, are built into a spiritual house on the chosen and precious cornerstone. It is a close parallel to verses 20 to 22 and adds that the stones form a holy priesthood, so the temple is also a company of priests.

Paul tells the Corinthians that they are God's temple and that God's Spirit dwells in them, and that destroying the temple will bring destruction. It supports the claim of verse 22 and adds a warning: those who damage the unity and holiness of the church are touching what God calls His own.

Jesus speaks of other sheep not of this fold whom He must bring in, so that there will be one flock and one shepherd. Ephesians 2 describes how the other sheep were brought in. The one flock does not erase the first fold but joins it.

Confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, through the curtain of His body. This gives the Jewish temple version of the access Paul calls prosagoge in verse 18, and shows that the way in is Christ's body.
God's dwelling place is with man, and He will dwell with them. The temple growing in Ephesians 2:21 to 22 is completed here, when the dwelling is no longer partial or still under construction.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture begins with one humanity made in God's image in one garden, and the first sin splits it: Adam and Eve hide from God and blame each other, Genesis 3:7 to 13. From there the divisions multiply. Cain separates from his brother, the builders at Babel are scattered into peoples and tongues, Genesis 11:8 to 9, and the nations drift from the true God. Ephesians 2:12 describes the result in one sentence: without hope and without God in the world.

God's answer begins at once and in a particular way. He calls Abraham so that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, Genesis 12:3, and sets Israel apart with covenant, law and temple, Leviticus 20:26. The wall Paul speaks of belongs to that design: it protected a people who were to carry the promise until the promised seed arrived. It was never meant to be permanent, and the prophets saw the nations streaming to the mountain of the LORD, Isaiah 2:2 to 3, and foreigners joining themselves to Him, Isaiah 56:6 to 7.

The cross is where the two stories meet. It deals with the sin that split humanity at the start and the barrier that guarded the promise. When Christ dies, the veil is torn, Matthew 27:51, and the wall comes down. At Pentecost the Spirit is poured out on people from many nations, Acts 2:5 to 11, and the first Gentile household receives the Spirit in Acts 10. Ephesians 2:11 to 22 is the explanation of what those events meant.

What comes after is the building. The temple is still growing, and the church's task in this age is to live out the peace that has been made. The vision at the end, Revelation 5:9 to 10 and 7:9, shows people from every tribe and language and people and nation before the throne, and Revelation 21:3 hears the voice that says God's dwelling place is with man. Babel's scattering is reversed, the garden's lost presence is restored, and the one new humanity that Paul saw rising in verses 21 and 22 stands complete.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe the Gentiles' former condition in verses 11 to 12?

options.text: Separate from Christ, alienated from Israel, strangers to the covenants, without hope and without God.
options.note: Paul piles up the terms of their exclusion so the reversal will shine all the brighter.

options.text: Slightly disadvantaged but basically near to God already.
options.note: Paul says they were far off, without hope and without God, not merely disadvantaged.

options.text: Members of Israel who had simply forgotten the covenants.
options.note: They were Gentiles in the flesh, outsiders to the commonwealth of Israel, not lapsed members.

options.text: Already reconciled and needing no change.
options.note: The whole point of but now in verse 13 is that a decisive change was needed and came.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean when he says Christ Himself is our peace?

options.text: Christ in His own person is the peace between God and man and between Jew and Gentile, not merely its negotiator.
options.note: He Himself is our peace, who made the two one; the peace is a reality created in Him.

options.text: Christ arranged a truce between two parties who then keep it themselves.
options.note: The peace is not a brokered treaty but a new reality created in His person at the cross.

options.text: Christ gives inner calm to individuals only.
options.note: The context is corporate: two peoples made one, both reconciled to God.

options.text: Christ leaves the old hostility in place.
options.note: He tore down the dividing wall and put the hostility to death through the cross.

quiz.q: What happened to the dividing wall of hostility at the cross?

options.text: Christ tore it down, abolishing in His flesh what kept Jew and Gentile apart.
options.note: The barrier that fenced the nations out is demolished in the flesh of Christ.

options.text: It was left standing but made a little lower.
options.note: Paul says it was torn down and the hostility put to death, not merely lowered.

options.text: It was rebuilt stronger to keep the peoples separate.
options.note: The movement is the opposite: from two into one new man.

options.text: It never existed in the first place.
options.note: Paul assumes a real division of law and custom that Christ has now removed.

quiz.q: According to verse 18, what do both Jew and Gentile now have through Christ?

options.text: Access to the Father by one Spirit.
options.note: Through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit, the whole Trinity in one clause.

options.text: Access to the Father earned by keeping the law.
options.note: Access comes through Christ and by the Spirit, not by law-keeping.

options.text: Access for Jews first and Gentiles only later.
options.note: Paul says we both have access together, by one Spirit.

options.text: No real access, only the hope of it one day.
options.note: The access is a present reality: we both have access to the Father.

quiz.q: What is the church becoming, according to verses 19 to 22?

options.text: A holy temple and dwelling place for God, built on the apostolic foundation with Christ as cornerstone.
options.note: Jew and Gentile fitted together grow into a holy sanctuary where God dwells by His Spirit.

options.text: A loose alliance of two peoples who remain essentially separate.
options.note: Paul says they are one new man, one body, one building, not a loose alliance.

options.text: A physical temple rebuilt in Jerusalem.
options.note: The temple here is a people knit together in Christ, not a building of stone.

options.text: A structure that stands without any need of Christ.
options.note: Christ is the cornerstone on whom the whole building is fitted together and rises.

quiz.q: Why does Paul begin by telling the Gentiles to remember?

options.text: So that grasping how far off they once were, they marvel at how near Christ has brought them.
options.note: Remembering the former estate magnifies the grace of the but now in verse 13.

options.text: So they feel permanently inferior to Jewish believers.
options.note: The aim is not lasting inferiority but shared wonder; both are now one new man with equal access.

options.text: So they return to keeping the ceremonial law.
options.note: Christ abolished the dividing law; the call is to remember grace, not resume the barrier.

options.text: So they take pride in their own achievement.
options.note: The passage removes all boasting; they were brought near by the blood of Christ.

questions: Paul tells the Gentiles to remember what they once were. How does remembering the distance you were once at from God deepen your gratitude for being brought near?
Christ Himself is our peace, not merely the one who arranges it. What difference does it make that peace with God is a person to be received rather than a state you must achieve?
The cross tore down the deepest dividing wall of the ancient world. What walls of hostility, in your church or relationships, is the gospel calling you to treat as already demolished in Christ?
Both Jew and Gentile now have access to the Father by one Spirit. How does this confidence of access shape the way you come to God in prayer?
You are being built together into a dwelling place for God. How does seeing the church as God's living temple change the way you view other believers and your own place among them?

translationNotes.note: The dividing wall renders mesotoichon, a middle wall of partition; many see an allusion to the temple barrier that excluded Gentiles from the inner courts, as well as to the whole hedge of law separating Israel from the nations.

The law of commandments and decrees is best read in context as the boundary-marking legislation that divided Jew from Gentile; whatever its precise scope, Paul's point is that Christ removed it to make one new man out of the two.

Cornerstone renders akrogoniaios, which can mean the foundational corner stone or the chief capstone; either way it is the decisive stone, Christ Himself, that aligns and binds the whole structure, fulfilling Isaiah 28:16 and Psalm 118:22.
